## Objectives {#objectives}

By the end of this session you can:

- Pull fields from a web page with `rvest` and CSS selectors.
- Follow pagination and confirm you collected every item.
- Decide whether a site may be scraped, from its terms of use, its
  robots.txt, copyright and any personal data on the page.
- Scrape without getting blocked by pausing between requests,
  identifying yourself, caching pages and backing off when the server
  asks.
- Have an AI coding agent write and run a scraper, then compare what it
  collected with the live pages.

## What we cover {#coverage}

- Published work built on web scraping, where a program reads pages
  built for people and copies chosen pieces into a table.
  [Cavallo (AER, 2017)](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20160542) built a
  scraping robot for each of 56 large retailers in 10 countries and
  compared their online prices with prices in the same retailers' stores.
  [Kuhn & Shen (QJE, 2013)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjs046)
  collected over a million ads from a Chinese online job board with a
  crawler (a program that follows links from page to page and saves each
  one) and measured how often employers ask for a particular gender.
  [Christensen & Timmins (QJE, 2023)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjad029)
  used a bot to collect every three-bedroom, two-bathroom rental listing
  on a major platform in five US cities, recorded toxic-pollution data
  for each, and sent inquiries from renters with distinct names to
  measure discrimination.
- `rvest` and CSS selectors. HTML is the text behind every web page,
  made of labelled pieces called elements, such as a heading, a link or
  a table cell. A CSS selector is a short pattern that picks out
  elements by label, class name or position. You find the element in
  the browser's inspector, the panel that shows the HTML behind whatever
  you point at, and pull its text into a data frame.
- The running example: the policy statements and press-conference
  transcripts the Federal Reserve posts after each meeting, collected by
  following the links on its meeting calendar.
- Pagination, a list split across numbered pages the scraper visits in
  turn. Compare the count you collected with the count the site shows,
  and open the last item next to its page, since a truncated scrape loses
  the end of the list.
- Whether scraping is allowed. Terms of use are a site's legal rules for
  visitors and may forbid automated copying. The robots.txt file at the
  site's main address lists pages automated programs are asked to skip.
  Copyright gives a creator control over copies of a work, though in the
  US bare facts such as prices are not covered. Personal data is anything
  that identifies a living person, such as a name or a photo. When an
  API exists or the data can be bought, use that instead.
- Avoiding blocks: a delay between requests, a user agent (the name your
  program sends with each request) that says who you are, and caching,
  saving every page to disk the first time so you never fetch it twice.
  When the server answers HTTP 429 ("too many requests"), back off by
  waiting longer after each refusal, often doubling the wait.
- An AI coding agent, a tool that writes and runs code on your computer
  from plain-language instructions, writes and runs the scraper. You
  then verify what it collected against the live pages.
